title: Why Does Java Run on Different Computers?
summary: Understand how intermediate bytecode and the JVM solve platform compatibility without rewriting code.
learningObjectives: Differentiate direct machine code (.exe) from portable bytecode (.class)
Understand why the JVM is platform-dependent while bytecode is portable
expectedOutcomes: Clear understanding of why Java code written on Windows runs seamlessly on Mac and Linux

activities.title: Why Does Java Run on Different Computers?

breakdown.whatIsIt: Java is famous for WORA: 'Write Once, Run Anywhere'. You can write your program on Windows, and the exact same compiled file runs on macOS or Linux without changes.
breakdown.whyItMatters: In older languages like C++, an executable compiled on Windows (.exe) crashes on a Mac because their processors and operating systems speak different binary formats. Java eliminates this limitation.
howItWorks: You write your program in Main.java.
The compiler (javac) turns your code into universal Bytecode (Main.class), which is independent of any operating system.
Each OS has its own JVM translator (Windows JVM, Mac JVM, Linux JVM). The local JVM reads the universal bytecode and translates it into native CPU instructions.
keyTakeaways: You never have to recompile your program for different laptops

activities.title: Cross-Platform Message Example
activities.description: This program prints Java's famous promise. When compiled, the resulting Main.class can be shared and run on any machine with Java installed.

questions.prompt: Which component of Java is platform-independent, and which is platform-dependent?
options: Bytecode is platform-independent; the JVM is platform-dependent
Bytecode is platform-dependent; the JVM is platform-independent
Both Bytecode and JVM are platform-independent
Both Bytecode and JVM are platform-dependent

hints.hint: Think about whether you download a different Java installer for Windows vs Mac.

questions.explanation: Bytecode (.class) is identical across all systems (Write Once). But the JVM must be tailored to the specific OS and CPU (Run Anywhere). Therefore, the JVM itself is platform-dependent.

activities.title: Hands-on Practice: Output the WORA Motto

practice.title: WORA Assignment
practice.problemStatement: Write a Java program that outputs: 'Write Once, Run Anywhere!' to standard output.
requirements: Include standard entry point: public static void main(String[] args)
Output must exactly match: Write Once, Run Anywhere!
hints: Double check spelling and exclamation mark.
Ensure the semicolon (;) is at the end of the line.

interviewQA.question: Why is Java called platform-independent?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java is platform-independent because its compiler produces intermediate Bytecode (.class) instead of machine-specific binary code. Any operating system equipped with a compatible Java Virtual Machine (JVM) can interpret and execute this bytecode without recompiling the original source code.
keyPoints: OS-specific JVM translates Bytecode to native machine instructions
Eliminates the need for OS-specific builds
commonMistakes: Claiming that the JVM itself is platform-independent

activities.title: Confidence Checklist
checklist: I can explain what WORA stands for and what it means.
I understand why bytecode is portable across Windows, Mac, and Linux.
I know that the JVM is OS-specific.
